items.title: Why a coin flip isn't 50/50
items.summary: A coin flip isn't 50/50. Researchers flipped coins 350,757 times. Heads and tails came out even at 0.500. But the side that started facing up landed up 50.8% of the time. A flipped coin wobbles, so it spends a little more time with the starting side up. A 2007 physics model by Diaconis, Holmes and Montgomery predicted about 51%. The 2023 data landed on 50.8%.Why a coin flip isn't 50/50. Researchers flipped coins 350,757 times. Heads and tails came out even, but the side that started facing up landed up 50.8% of the time, because a flipped coin wobbles. Source: Bartos et al. 2023, "Fair coins tend to land on the same side they started" (arXiv 2310.04153). Prediction: Diaconis, Holmes and Montgomery 2007. Idea: Mark Rober. Call it before you flip: same side or the other? #Shorts #coinflip #probability Idea: Mark Rober. Sources: Bartos et al. 2023, "Fair coins tend to land on the same side they started" (arXiv 2310.04153). Diaconis, Holmes and Montgomery 2007. Call it before you flip: same side or the other?

items.title: When will the Sun die?
items.summary: Our Sun is about halfway through its life. The Sun formed about 4.6 billion years ago and is a little less than halfway through its life. In about 5 billion years it becomes a red giant that swallows Mercury and Venus, with Earth the open question. Then it sheds its outer layers and leaves a white dwarf that cools for billions of years. Idea: Cleo Abram. Source: NASA Science (Sun facts, Stars). Footage: Storyblocks, NASA, and a Hubble image of the Ring Nebula (NASA, ESA, C. Robert O'Dell). The star chart is a schematic. If Earth gets swallowed, where do you go?
